items.title: Ukraine Says It Received No Intelligence About Strikes 2 Nights in a Row
items.summary: Asked about apparent U.S. threats to cut off intelligence sharing with Kyiv, which can warn of Russian aerial attacks, President Trump said information continued to flow.
items.full_text:
Title: Ukraine Says It Received No Intelligence About Strikes 2 Nights in a Row - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/world/europe/ukraine-trump-intelligence.html

Published Time: Tue, 13 Oct 2026 21:27:47 GMT

Markdown Content:
Ukraine said it received no warning from its Western partners before a Russian missile attack against Kyiv on Tuesday night, after reporting earlier in the day that it had gotten no intelligence about a round of strikes the night before.

The news raised fears in Ukraine that the Trump administration had made good on apparent threats to cut off intelligence sharing that includes alerts of such attacks, even as both U.S. and Ukrainian officials asserted that intelligence continued to flow.

Before the latest Russian attack on Kyiv, President Trump said Tuesday that the United ⁠States was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine. “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” he [told reporters](https://x.com/RapidResponse47/status/2110033106384142578?s=20) who had asked him about the possibility of cutting off intelligence if Kyiv did not halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.

The Ukrainian foreign minister also said on Tuesday that intelligence sharing was continuing, asserting that the attack the night before went undetected “because of a special type of weaponry which was used by the Russian side.”

Mr. Zelensky then weighed in again late on Tuesday, after the second ballistic missile attack. “Russian missile strike on Kyiv,” he [wrote on social media](https://x.com/ZelenskyyUa/status/2110104163967246529). “Once again, no warning from our partners.”

He called the situation “absolutely unjust,” adding that Russia was “destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches.”

Commenting on the first attack, some military experts said there may have been no warning simply because it was not detected before launch, which has happened in the past, and not because of the United States withholding intelligence.

Russia has previously fired missiles that Western satellites have struggled to track, including S-400 missiles, which Ukraine has at times described as ballistic weapons. Serhiy Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Mr. Zelensky, [said after the attack](https://t.me/serhii_flash/7804) on Monday that it was not the first time Western partners had failed to detect a launch of S-400 missiles.

Still, it would be unusual for Kyiv’s Western allies to fail to detect two missile attacks in a row.

Fears that Washington might cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine emerged after Mr. Trump [struck a deal](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/us/politics/trump-russia-diesel-putin.html) with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to buy millions of tons of Russian fuel. The agreement is part of an effort to bring down sky-high diesel prices, caused mostly by the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, before the U.S. midterm elections.

As they [presented the deal to the Ukrainians](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/world/europe/russia-ukraine-war-us-diesel-deal-negotiations.html) at a meeting last week in Miami, Trump administration officials asked Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries so that Russian diesel could flow back onto the market. They said Kyiv owed Washington for critical U.S. intelligence assistance, which some in the room took as a veiled threat. A U.S. official later denied any suggestion that intelligence support would be withheld.

Image

Mr. Zelensky spoke by video link to the Warsaw Security Forum, in Poland, on Monday.Credit...Wojtek Radwanski/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Mr. Zelensky said Ukraine had refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries over the past two days, framing it as a gesture of good will toward Mr. Trump, who on Friday declared an energy cease-fire that [neither Kyiv nor Moscow has confirmed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/15/world/europe/trump-energy-truce-ukraine-russia.html).

Ukraine has warned that such a cease-fire would work only if Russia stopped its attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities. Russia has continued to strike power plants even after Mr. Trump declared an energy cease-fire, Kyiv says. Mr. Zelensky said Tuesday night’s strike targeted a combined heat-and-power plant supplying Kyiv.

“The facts show that the Russians do not consider themselves bound by what the President of the United States said,” he wrote on social media. “Ukraine supported an energy cease-fire. Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people.”

The Trump administration has shown before that it is willing to withhold intelligence as a lever against Ukraine. After a White House meeting in which Mr. Trump berated Mr. Zelensky in front of journalists in early 2025, Washington [paused intelligence sharing with Ukraine](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/05/us/politics/cia-director-ukraine-intelligence.html?eafs_enabled=false) for a few days.

On Monday, Russian missiles struck Kyiv around 10 p.m. local time. Air-raid alerts sounded too late, after the missiles had been launched, leaving residents with no warning. The lapse immediately prompted speculation online that Washington had halted intelligence sharing. Air-raid alerts sounded late, again, in the attack on Tuesday.

Ukraine lacks the extensive satellite-based intelligence capabilities of the United States and relies on information from Western partners to monitor Russian military preparations signaling an attack. That includes activity at air bases, movements of ships and the deployment of ballistic missile launchers.

“Our NATO partners inform us when there is activity involving strategic aviation. Flights from one airfield to another. Where missiles are being delivered,” Col. Yurii Ihnat, a Ukrainian Air Force spokesman, said in an interview this summer. Sometimes, he added, Western satellites detected a flash indicating a missile launch, and partners immediately informed Ukraine.

Commenting on the Monday attack, Colonel Ihnat [told](https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=ym45iAmBOjYiTUHW&v=FK37rPakk70&feature=youtu.be) Ukrainian national television that Western intelligence sometimes “fails to arrive.”

“This is not the first case,” he said. “If there were certain technical issues this time, I believe the experts can sort it out. And we will resolve this problem together with our partners.”

Mr. Zelensky said Western intelligence was critical. “This is what helps prevent killings when there is a warning about ballistic missiles,” he said in a [social media post](https://t.me/V_Zelenskiy_official/21349) on Tuesday.

The cost of missing early warnings is perhaps felt most keenly in the eastern Ukrainian city of [Kharkiv](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/15/world/europe/kharkiv-ukraine-russia-photos.html?eafs_enabled=false), which lies only about 20 miles from the Russian border. Air-raid alerts sometimes cannot be sounded fast enough when Russia attacks the city.

Image

A firefighter at the site of the strike in Kharkiv on Monday,Credit...Mauricio Lima for The New York Times

On Monday night, volleys of drones hit Kharkiv, rocking the city center with loud, rumbling explosions. Fires burned in several locations. One strike tore into a residential building, collapsing apartments to the ground. The mayor, Ihor Terekhov, said in a [social media post](https://t.me/ihor_terekhov/4783) that four people had been killed on Monday and that two more strikes hit the city the next day.

On Tuesday, rescuers who worked through the night were still at the site of the residential building, pulling a body from the wreckage. Exhausted firefighters rested on the open trunks of vehicles as bulldozers cleared blackened rubble of bricks and belongings. A burning smell hung in the air.

Lyubov Smal, 69, one of the residents, with stitches on cuts to her face, said she had been cooking cutlets in her kitchen when a drone struck the building.

Bleeding, she made her way through smoke to the landing and was helped out by firefighters. Twelve hours later, she came back to plead for help in finding her cat. Resting from working through the night, two rescuers jumped up and climbed the blackened stairs to a third-floor apartment.

“He won’t bite us?” they jokingly asked. Minutes later, they were back with a big gray cat with yellow eyes. He dug his claws into the fleece of a neighbor, jumping at loud noises as bulldozers resumed clearing rubble.

Image

Residents watching rescuers working on the apartment building damaged by the strike in Kharkiv.Credit...Mauricio Lima for The New York Times

Kamila Hrabchuk contributed reporting from Kharkiv.

items.title: Lawyer for Fed Governor Cook Denounces Trump’s New Investigation
items.summary: A lawyer for Lisa Cook raised “significant concerns” over the “objectivity and fitness of the committee” assembled by President Trump as a way to remove her as a governor at the Federal Reserve.
items.full_text:
Title: Lawyer for Fed Governor Cook Denounces Trump’s New Investigation - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/business/fed-governor-lisa-cook-trump-investigation.html

Published Time: Tue, 13 Oct 2026 21:33:06 GMT

Markdown Content:
Lisa D. Cook on Tuesday challenged President Trump’s [latest attempt](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/business/trump-lisa-cook-fed.html) to remove her from her role as a Federal Reserve governor, questioning the objectivity of a White House investigation into unproven allegations that she committed mortgage fraud.

In a letter to the White House viewed by The New York Times, Ms. Cook’s lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said the governor would not be able to attend a hearing scheduled for Nov. 5 because she would be fulfilling her duties in Europe “at financial and monetary policy meetings.”

Mr. Lowell said the earliest that any hearing could take place was after the Fed’s policy meeting scheduled for Dec. 8-9.

Mr. Lowell also questioned the objectivity of the investigation, which will be run by a committee that is staffed with Mr. Trump’s political appointees, including Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council; Keith Sonderling, the Labor secretary who is serving as acting director of a government ethics office; and Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

“We have significant concerns regarding the objectivity and fitness of the committee for its assigned purpose,” Mr. Lowell said.

Mr. Trump, who has long sought more control over the central bank in a bid to lower borrowing costs, has signaled how he expects the committee to rule. When asked on Friday about the investigation into Ms. Cook, the president called her “dishonest” and said that if the committee found that there was cause to remove her, he would “absolutely” fire her.

“A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence — with no explanation for why it was not previously produced — is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence,” Mr. Lowell said.

The decision to create a committee comes on the heels of a [Supreme Court ruling](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/06/29/us/politics/supreme-court-decision-trump-lisa-cook.html) that denied Mr. Trump the right to fire Ms. Cook after his initial attempt in August 2025. The justices in June [ruled](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/29/us/politics/trump-fire-fed-governor-cook.html) 5 to 4 in favor of Ms. Cook remaining in her job while litigation progressed, but they shied away from engaging in the substance of the claims against her and focused instead on procedural issues.

Mr. Trump quickly seized on that opening, announcing immediately after the Supreme Court ruling that he would continue his campaign against Ms. Cook, who has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime despite the allegations being more than a year old.

On the surface, the investigation into Ms. Cook appears to comply with the Supreme Court’s demands that the Trump administration provide the Fed governor ample opportunity to respond and defend herself before proceeding with her ouster.

In a memo dated Oct. 7, the White House stipulated the scope of the investigation, detailed who from the administration would staff it, and declared deadlines for Ms. Cook to submit supporting documents and written statements. It also summoned her to attend the in-person hearing, warning that this could include questioning from Department of Justice personnel.

Christina Skinner, who recently stepped down as an official at the Treasury Department and is now back at the University of Pennsylvania as a professor, described the process as “robust,” noting that the president pulled in people from “different facets of the White House ecosystem,” while also giving Ms. Cook “several avenues” to respond.

But for Ms. Cook’s lawyers, the current setup falls far short.

One of their primary concerns centers on the people who Mr. Trump tapped for the committee.

Mr. Hassett, the president’s top economic adviser, has joined with Mr. Trump in frequent criticism of the Fed, which he recently faulted for an “unusually partisan” board after it chose to raise interest rates to control inflation, rather than cut them as the president has demanded.

He had been among the finalists to lead the central bank under Mr. Trump, but the president opted to keep Mr. Hassett in his current post because he viewed him as a reliable, vocal advocate for his agenda.

In the weeks after the administration first accused Ms. Cook of engaging in mortgage fraud, Mr. Hassett defended the power of the president to fire a Fed governor if he determines there is cause to do so. Last fall, Mr. Hassett described the allegations against Ms. Cook as “serious” and called on Ms. Cook to take a leave of absence until they were resolved.

“The fact she’s not doing that now suggests she’s being partisan,” Mr. Hassett told reporters.

In his letter, Mr. Lowell pointed to past comments made by Mr. Hassett, noting that he “already has publicly insinuated that the President has ‘cause’ to fire Governor Cook.”

Mr. Sonderling, for his part, had previously endorsed Mr. Trump’s views on interest rates, echoing to CNBC recently that the Fed “should cut interest rates.” The Fed’s decision to raise rates came amid stubborn inflation that has exceeded the central bank’s 2 percent target for nearly six years.

Ms. Lucas has carried out Mr. Trump’s agenda at the E.E.O.C., chiefly by undoing what she has described as aggressive attempts by liberals to pursue diversity, equity and inclusion policies in the workplace. She has particularly focused on corporate discrimination against white male workers.

items.title: F.B.I. Arrests OpenAI Employee Accused of Planting Bug in Office
items.summary: OpenAI said that the employee had placed a device built to evade detection and that he had planned to secretly record meetings in other sensitive spaces.
items.full_text:
Title: F.B.I. Arrests OpenAI Employee Accused of Planting Bug in Office - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/technology/openai-worker-arrested-bugging.html

Published Time: Tue, 13 Oct 2026 22:00:38 GMT

Markdown Content:
OpenAI [said](https://x.com/OpenAINewsroom/status/2110095403198849132) on Tuesday that it had discovered a hidden recording device in one of its offices and traced it to an employee, and that the Federal Bureau of Investigation had arrested the worker.

A team that searches for surveillance equipment found the device on Sept. 30 during a sweep of a conference room, OpenAI said. The device was built to evade detection, used advanced encryption, could monitor audio and had a way to transfer data without being noticed, the company said.

The employee planned to place more recording devices in sensitive areas of the artificial intelligence company’s offices to secretly record meetings, it added. OpenAI said it had used its most advanced A.I. models to help investigators analyze copies of the device’s stored data and track changes to it.

The Department of Justice [identified the employee](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/saudi-national-arrested-installing-surreptitious-audio-recording-device-openai) as a Saudi Arabian national, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35. Mr. Alfozan, who joined OpenAI’s product team in July 2025 as an engineer, was fired on Friday, the day he was arrested, the company said. The device was inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in one of OpenAI’s buildings in San Francisco, according to the Justice Department.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code or customer data,” OpenAI said in a statement.

Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence at the Justice Department, said in a statement, “This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative — and why President Trump’s leadership in creating the Super Intelligence Force is so important.”

Kash Patel, F.B.I. director, said protecting U.S. tech innovation was “essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security.”

The incident adds to longstanding concerns about the security of leading A.I. labs, which create cutting-edge models and conduct research that are among the most closely guarded assets in the tech industry. The rapid pace of A.I. advancement has thrust many A.I. companies into a debate over the safety of the technology, with some A.I. leaders saying foundational models are progressing too quickly and can be dangerous, especially in the wrong hands.

OpenAI has faced scrutiny over security before. In 2023, a hacker broke into the company’s [messaging systems](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/04/technology/openai-hack.html) and stole details about the design of its A.I. technologies.

More recently, OpenAI’s advanced A.I. models have gone rogue, hacking into the A.I. start-up Hugging Face and an Australian government website without the company’s knowledge. Some [OpenAI employees had cautioned executives](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/technology/openai-warnings-security.html) to take more care in testing the advanced models, The New York Times has reported.

In its statement on Tuesday, OpenAI said that protecting its technology was “a matter of national importance,” and that its security program was built to guard against threats from insiders, cybercriminals and nation-states.

OpenAI said it had timed the firing of its employee with the F.B.I. to avoid disrupting the investigation. It gradually limited the employee’s access to company systems and offices, then suspended his access, put him on leave and took his company equipment.

Mr. Alfozan appeared in federal court in San Francisco on Tuesday, the Justice Department said.

(The Times [sued](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/12/27/business/media/new-york-times-open-ai-microsoft-lawsuit.html) OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, accusing them of copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)
